title: Swadeshi Clusters: Familial bonds of prosperity
excerpt: Swadeshi’s is the outward, practical manifestation of patriotism. Patriotism is not considered as isolationism—particularly in our tradition, which stands for integral humanism according to which, on the level of human consciousness, internationalism is the further flowering of the spirit of nationalism. Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that presenting patriotism as isolationism is the usual practice of imperialist powers. …Patriots are not against internationalism. Their plea for national self-reliance is not incompatible with international co-operation, provided the latter is on equal footing—with due regard to the national self-respect of every country. Their difference of opinion with the advocates of ‘globalisation’ is on a different and more basic point – Dattopant Thengadi, Swadeshi is the Practical Manifestation of Patriotism, GLOBALISATION, LIBERALISATION AND ‘SWADESHI’—I, Organiser Weekly, December 26, 1993 According to the World Bank’s Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026, Bharat has lifted an estimated 496 million people above the poverty threshold. The report estimates that Bharat’s multidimensional extreme poverty fell from 27.1 per cent in 2011 to 2.6 per cent in 2023, which is a remarkable feat for us as a nation. Since the 2008 banking crisis in the US, doomsday predictors have missed the real strength of Bharat that sustains us beyond global crises. Unless we decode the civilisational strength of Bharat, in which community bonds, sustainability concerns, the cycle of festivities, human-centric supply chains and the concept of shared prosperity are all interwoven in a beautiful fabric, we cannot understand the secret behind this success of Bharat as a shining star amidst global uncertainties. A common cliché calls Bharat an agrarian country with a rural setting. This narration assumes that a village means agricultural activities. The pre-British period completely nullifies this assumption. The OECD-supported research by Angus Maddison titled The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective clearly shows that Bharat held a major share of the world economy for centuries. A society that believed in not selling food grains could not account for a quarter of global GDP solely through agrarian produce. Villages functioned as industrial clusters, with local communities possessing specialised skills and optimising resource use, making this model possible. Generational skill transfer, trust-based transactions, and the ability to stay connected with the world while remaining hyperlocal in lifestyle allow these clusters to absorb global shocks. Domestic demand and the supply chain remain a handy cushion. They share the burden of hard work, as well as the fruits of prosperity. Community-based collective industry, which addresses environmental concerns, is at the heart of this model. Even though , through inhuman exploitation, broke the backbone of the Bharatiya economy for their capitalist interests, some clusters still survived the onslaught with local demand and supply chains. For instance, the leather industry faced major social and economic challenges due to colonial policies, but the silk industry in some sectors survived. Even the mindless imitation of socialism and quota-permit raj could not affect the autonomous character of these clusters. Imposed globalisation brought initial challenges, but these resilient communities accepted them and turned the pressure into opportunities to explore export avenues. If we look at the reverse-engineering skills of Gadia Lohars, no trained engineer can match them. Tiruppur, known as the ‘Knitwear Capital’ or ‘Dollar City ’, is driven by the skills of the Kongu Vellalar Gounder community. The Patidars of Morbi have maintained one of the world’s biggest ceramic-exporting hubs. The Marwaris and Sindhis bring similar expertise to the trading sector. Irrespective of qualifications, these communities bring specialised skill sets and add a unique model of shared wealth creation. The modern education system and development parameters do not recognise these specificities and therefore fail to understand Bharat. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the Finance Ministry of Bharat also recognised the importance of these clusters and, with a few more modern tech-based additions, provided new momentum to this approach. Through the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI), traditional artisans and producers are being brought into collectives to boost competitiveness, provide infrastructure, explore designs, and ensure market access. Under the scheme, over 513 clusters have been approved nationwide, benefiting more than 3.03 lakh artisans in sectors like handicrafts, handloom, coir, agro-processing, and honey. The India Crafts Cluster Portal (ICCP) showcases thousands of artisan-made products under the Ministry of Textiles, which includes GI-tagged products from Varanasi (Uttar Pradesh), Kanchipuram (Tamil Nadu), Kutch (Gujarat), Pochampally (Telangana), Srinagar (Jammu & Kashmir), Bhagalpur (Bihar), Nalbari (Assam), and Jaipur (Rajasthan), to name a few. They testify to the community activities of artisans from all corners of Bharat who make substantial contributions to the economy. They are not the residual but the real drivers of the Bharatiya growth story. Bharat should and will explore high-tech sectors, including space and Artificial Intelligence, without neglecting traditional cluster models. They are the ones allowing us to sustain and grow amidst global upheavals. Swadeshi as a philosophy is not just about buying indigenous products but creating sustainable cluster models across the globe. This model generates local employment based on natural skills and talent passed down from generation to generation. It strengthens the communitarian bonds and family values, and mindless urbanisation is not a sustainable parameter of development. Regardless of gender, each family member is involved in some activity in the procurement, production, or supply chain, bringing meaningful employment. They are the real confluence of rural settings and urban amenities, leading to the RURBAN model. These models are inherently sustainable because they rely more on the local supply chain and use less fuel. These models can absorb global external shocks because of localised finance systems and the trust factor within the community when it comes to credit lines. Cooperation is the natural spirit, along with healthy competition among the units, since they are interdependent in many ways. They adapt to technological and global expectations while still catering to local demand and supply chains. Shared resources and shared prosperity are the two dots of the circle that make these models self-sufficient and more egalitarian. title: Periyar Library Book Row: AI Content, Price Markups & TVK-DMK Political Showdown
excerpt: A controversy over book purchases for Tamil Nadu's Periyar library has triggered a political storm, with allegations of inflated prices, questionable authors and possible AI-generated content. Sahitya Akademi awardee Perumal Murugan has flagged alleged irregularities in around 1,800 books, including factual errors, unverified registration numbers, missing publisher details and suspicious price tags. One book reportedly priced at ₹250 carried a price tag exceeding ₹1,500. The issue has now become a political flashpoint between the ruling TVK government and the opposition DMK. Tamil Nadu Minister Raj Mohan has promised an inquiry, while DMK leaders have questioned the credibility of the books. With Kamal Haasan also demanding action, the key question is: what happened in the Periyar library book procurement process?

title: From Homi Bhabha to Vikram Sarabhai: Tracing shadows, sabotage, espionage & mysterious death of scientists of Bharat
excerpt: A nation’s success hinges on placing a high value on research and innovation. This entails honouring scientists, researchers, innovators and skilled individuals for their contributions and ensuring their safety against potential threats from international organizations and anti-national elements attempting to undermine their national work. Unfortunately, prior to 2014, our scientific and research community experienced a challenging period that hindered progress in several areas, including nuclear technology. Let’s review the negative events that impacted our esteemed scientific community. In response to a 2015 Right to Information (RTI) request, government data indicated that between 2009 and 2013, at least 11 nuclear scientists and technicians experienced unnatural deaths—ranging from mysterious fires to suspected homicides and drownings—at facilities such as the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and Nuclear Power Corporation of Bharat (NPCIL). Over a wider span of 15 years (1995–2010), the total number of reported deaths among personnel of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) under suspicious circumstances exceeded 60 to 70 cases, although many were officially deemed suicides or accidents. Similarly, numerous researchers involved in defense projects, missile propulsion, and satellite systems have also died under unexplained circumstances, including homicides or sudden deaths that were not autopsied. Mysterious deaths of notable scientists, including Dr. Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai On January 24, 61 years ago, Homi Bhabha tragically lost his life when Air Bharat Flight 101 crashed near Mont Blanc while he was en route to a conference in Vienna. Many suspect that the crash was not accidental but rather a deliberate assassination orchestrated by American intelligence agencies aimed at undermining Bharat’s nuclear ambitions. Homi Jehangir Bhabha, often called the “Father of the Bharatiya Nuclear Programme,” is regarded as one of Bharat’s most brilliant minds. He was the founding director of the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay (now known as the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre) in his honor. Air India Flight 101 went down near Mont Blanc in the Swiss Alps soon after Bhabha announced that Bharat had the capability to develop a nuclear weapon. The notion of foul play gained traction following the release of a conversation between journalist Gregory Douglas and former CIA operative Robert T. Crowley, published by TBRNews.org in a book titled ‘Conversations with the Crow.’ This transcript suggested a potential CIA involvement in the ‘accident.’ Within the conversation, Crowley remarked, “We had issues with Bharat back in the 60s when they became assertive in developing an atomic bomb… They were cozying up to the Russians.” He referred to Bhabha as a dangerous figure, claiming, “He had an unfortunate accident. He was traveling to Vienna to create more complications when a bomb went off in the cargo hold of his Boeing 707.” Crowley’s ambiguous language sparked significant discussion, notably because if an explosion occurred on the flight, it could hardly be characterized as merely an “unfortunate accident.” The puzzling death of Vikram Sarabhai, known as the father of Bharat’s space program, occurred on December 30, 1971, when he was discovered deceased in his hotel room at Halcyon Castle in Kovalam. He had appeared to be in good health the night before while engaging in discussions with scientists, yet he was found dead the following morning. Dr. Narayanan seems to believe that international forces may have played a role in Sarabhai’s demise. In his biography, he states, “The challenges and questions surrounding his death are numerous. If he was indeed eliminated, it suggests the existence of an international conspiracy. How else could such a brilliant scientific mind die in such an unnatural way?” Narayanan, who closely collaborated with Sarabhai as a junior scientist at ISRO, dedicates a whole chapter to him in his book. He describes Sarabhai as “a man who had never smoked and was a teetotaler”. He questions how Sarabhai could have met such an end and why an autopsy wasn’t conducted, despite his significant contributions to science. He also references a conversation involving Crowley, highlighting that the Bharatiya victory in the 1965 Bharat-Pakistan war caused unease in America, which was concerned about Bharat emerging as a nuclear power. The book suggests that Bharat’s nuclear aspirations were potentially sabotaged without leaving any evidence, implying that Sarabhai’s death and the ISRO spy case create a troubling narrative. Scientists who succumbed to death under mysterious circumstances On June 13, 2009, Bharatiya television channels reported the death of Lokanathan Mahalingam, a relatively obscure nuclear scientist. Mahalingam had spent eight years at the Kaiga atomic power station in Karnataka, which is near the significant military base Project Seabird. This facility, operated by the Nuclear Power Corporation of Bharat since March 2000, includes four of eight nuclear reactors categorized as strategic, exempt from International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards prior to the “civilian nuclear cooperation agreement” with the US. Kaiga is located near Bharat’s principal naval base, INS Kadamba. On June 8, 2009, the 47-year-old senior scientific officer went for a morning walk and did not return. His decomposed body was discovered in the Kali River five days later, but his mysterious death received little attention in the Bharatiya media. Notably, five years earlier, an armed group had attempted to abduct an official from Bharat’s Nuclear Power Corporation in the same forest where Mahalingam’s body was found, although the official managed to escape. Another Nuclear Power Corporation employee, Ravi Mule, went missing and was later confirmed murdered. His family sought to investigate the case after law enforcement made little progress. On February 23, 2010, M. Iyer, an engineer from the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, was found dead in his home. The police investigation encountered obstacles, and forensic experts reported no fingerprints or evidence to identify any suspects, much like other unexplained deaths of those involved in Bharat’s nuclear sector. title: India targets indigenous GPU development in 2 years to boost semiconductor ambitions
excerpt: New Delhi, Nov 9 (IANS) India is aiming to develop its own graphics processing unit (GPU) within the next two years as part of a broader strategy to strengthen domestic semiconductor capabilities and reduce reliance on foreign chipmakers, according to Electronics and Information Technology Secretary S. Krishnan. Speaking in an interview, Krishnan said the government plans to pursue the project under the upcoming India Semiconductor Mission 2.0. He acknowledged that developing a homegrown GPU would be a complex undertaking but said the government has set a target of achieving the milestone within roughly 24 months. India has already made progress in AI-related hardware manufacturing. Companies such as VVDN Technologies, Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technologies are producing servers domestically, while the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) has developed its Rudra server platforms for AI workloads. Custom Ad: Multiplex Meanwhile, earlier this month, Amitesh Kumar Sinha, Additional Secretary at the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and CEO of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) said that India's semiconductor strategy has moved from policy design to building the ecosystem with early manufacturing projects already underway. Speaking on the second day and final day of the ISIG Executive Summit India 2026 on November 5, Sinha said India has approved 12 manufacturing projects, of which five have already begun commercial production. “Semicon 2.0 is about building the broader ecosystem, including design companies, materials, chemicals, gases and equipment, alongside manufacturing, R&D and talent,” he said. India's semiconductor ambitions have gained momentum in recent years with major global companies committing investments in the country. Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML is partnering with Tata Electronics to support India's first commercial semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat. The fab is expected to use 300mm wafers and eventually achieve a production capacity of 50,000 wafers per month. Intel has also entered into a strategic partnership with the Tata Group covering semiconductor manufacturing and packaging activities. --IANS pk

title: India targets indigenous GPU development in 2 years to boost semiconductor ambitions
excerpt: India is aiming to develop its own graphics processing unit (GPU) within the next two years as part of a broader strategy to strengthen domestic semiconductor capabilities and reduce reliance on foreign chipmakers, according to Electronics and Information Technology Secretary S. Krishnan. Speaking in an interview, Krishnan said the government plans to pursue the project under the upcoming India Semiconductor Mission 2.0. He acknowledged that developing a homegrown GPU would be a complex undertaking but said the government has set a target of achieving the milestone within roughly 24 months. India has already made progress in AI-related hardware manufacturing. Companies such as VVDN Technologies, Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technologies are producing servers domestically, while the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) has developed its Rudra server platforms for AI workloads. Meanwhile, earlier this month, Amitesh Kumar Sinha, Additional Secretary at the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and CEO of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) said that India's semiconductor strategy has moved from policy design to building the ecosystem with early manufacturing projects already underway. Speaking on the second day and final day of the ISIG Executive Summit India 2026 on November 5, Sinha said India has approved 12 manufacturing projects, of which five have already begun commercial production."Semicon 2.0 is about building the broader ecosystem, including design companies, materials, chemicals, gases and equipment, alongside manufacturing, R&D and talent," he said. India's semiconductor ambitions have gained momentum in recent years with major global companies committing investments in the country. Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML is partnering with Tata Electronics to support India's first commercial semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat. The fab is expected to use 300mm wafers and eventually achieve a production capacity of 50,000 wafers per month. Intel has also entered into a strategic partnership with the Tata Group covering semiconductor manufacturing and packaging activities.

title: 57-year-old Ketan Sodha turns failed crop into Rs 44 lakh soilless strawberry farming success
excerpt: Ketan Sodha began strawberry farming in Mahabaleshwar with no experience, facing failure in his initial attempt. He persisted and eventually expanded his business, learning about soilless cultivation techniques. Travelers to various countries helped him understand better practices suited to Indian conditions. His farm produced a significant yield and high sales, leading to plans for further expansion. Sodha's journey highlights the importance of adaptation and innovation in agriculture.
